newsitem.title: UK: Dollar mixed in late Europe, gains on sterling.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed in late Europe, gains on sterling.

text.p: The dollar steadied in late Europe after a volatile session as the market absorbed strong fourth-quarter U.S. economic growth but with mild underlying inflation.
"It's the same old story -- strong growth, but subdued inflation," said John Calverley, chief economist and strategist at American Express Bank in London.
Gross domestic product (GDP) jumped 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter, exceeding expectations of 3.9 percent and nearly double third-quarter growth.
But this was offset by a price index of 1.8 percent versus a consensus forecast of 2.2 percent.

"The dollar is just sort of consolidating," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS. "Today's data is just an excuse to maintain that," he said adding that many dealers had taken profits and closed their books for the month.

The day's data releases included the January University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey, which came in near forecast at 97.4 percent vs. 96.9 percent previously. The January Chicago purchasing managers index was at forecast of 57.4 percent.
U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television that the data showed the economy growing "substantially" with the strong dollar helping subdue inflation.
While strong, the figures would not change the U.S. interest rate outlook, analysts said.
"There is cause for a modest rate hike in the first half of the year, but no evidence for more than that," von Maydell said. "There is no evidence of an unbalanced economy."

Calverley said last Wednesday's employment cost index (ECI) -- which rose 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter -- was the week's crucial indicator because it showed wage costs in the United States were not rising strongly.
"That is what the Federal Reserve is really worried about," he said. "Wage costs will ultimately feed through to prices."
The dollar briefly surged above 1.64 marks and touched 1.22 yen after the bullish GDP figure, but then settled back as the market absorbed the favourable inflation figures, dealers said.
At 1650 GMT the dollar traded mid-range at 1.6370/80 marks versus 1.6357/67 in late Europe on Thursday. Dollar/yen was at 121.25/30 compared to 121.50/60 previously.

U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bundesbank Council Member Guntram Palm were reported to have said the yen's current level would be a major topic at the upcoming G7 finance ministers' meeting in Berlin.
This helped underpin the yen, dealers said.
G7 deputy finance ministers are expected to meet on Monday in Frankfurt ahead of the main event to discuss the dollar's steep rise and the health of the world economy.
But analysts questioned whether the G7 would take any concerted action to halt the dollar's climb against the yen and the mark.

"The only country that partly expressed some concern about the dollar is Japan, but even they seem divided," said UBS's von Maydell. "The simple fact is that the mark is still overvalued. It is going to continue to decline," he added.
